Came out of a long iterative design conversation that walked through several alternatives before landing on Caddy + process-compose + a thin Python CLI. Verified end-to-end on `hermes-vmendi-webapps` (CH Sandbox), then merged to main and torn down. A follow-up bugfix landed after `hermes-vmendi00` started 403'ing on `/api/session/new`.

**Why this design.** Constraint: the URL has to be on the agent's own hostname (no DNS/ALB rules per app). That means *something inside the container* must recognize `/webapps/<slug>` as non-WebUI traffic. Walked through five shapes before picking one: (a) static-only via WebUI patch — too narrow, no Elixir/Phoenix; (b) ASGI-mount inside WebUI — works for Python only, language-coupling; (c) Python reverse-proxy patch in WebUI — ~200 lines but every Hermes bump becomes a patch-conflict risk; (d) fd-handoff via `SCM_RIGHTS` (inetd-style) — elegant but founders on HTTP/1.1 keep-alive (one connection, many requests, different paths) and HTTP/2 multiplexing; (e) eBPF sockmap — likely blocked on Fargate, HTTP parsing in eBPF is rough. Caddy as a sidecar reverse proxy on 8787 won: zero WebUI patches, native WS / SSE / streaming, single ~40MB binary, no patch-conflict tax on Hermes bumps. The architectural lesson: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive + HTTP/2 fundamentally make L7 routing a per-*request* decision, not per-*connection* — anything that wants to stay out of the data path either pins one backend per connection (breaks the model) or pushes parsing into the kernel (overkill). Caddy is already optimal at the things that matter (`splice(2)`, native HTTP/2 demux, WS upgrades), so its data-path cost is fine.

**Trust boundary placement.** Caddy and process-compose run *inside* the existing nono sandbox alongside WebUI, as `hermeswebui`. Followed the rule: "outside nono only for processes that hold secrets the LLM mustn't read" (`aws_signer`, `integrations_broker`). Caddy's config is derived from agent-written files, so putting Caddy outside nono would mean a root-owned process consuming attacker-influenceable input — the worst trust direction. Inside nono, a Caddy CVE escalates to `hermeswebui`, same level the LLM already has.

**Process supervision: don't write our own.** First sketch had a 250-line Python `doh_appd.py` watching `/workspace/webapps/apps/*.yaml` and translating to a supervisor. Off-the-shelf candidates considered: s6, supervisord, runit, process-compose. Picked **process-compose** because (i) `process-compose project update -f process-compose.yaml` does surgical reload — only changed processes restart, new ones start, removed ones stop, readiness probes honored on reload; (ii) MCP server is a wrapper around CLI and `project update` covered everything we needed (skipped MCP); (iii) it's a single Go binary so the install is just a tarball download in the Dockerfile. The "we should write our own watcher" instinct was wrong — process-compose's "reload by editing YAML + run `project update`" is a clean checkpoint the agent can verify.

**Source-of-truth shape.** `/workspace/webapps/{process-compose.yaml, caddy/<slug>.caddy, projects/<slug>/, logs/<slug>.log}`. Caddy `--watch` picks up snippet add/remove on filesystem change; process-compose `project update` is invoked explicitly by the CLI. Originally proposed a directory of per-app YAMLs (filesystem-shaped agent UX), then switched to a single `process-compose.yaml` once we picked process-compose — its native shape, no translator needed. The agent never edits YAML directly; it goes through the `webapps` CLI for all mutations. CLI surface ended up at: `create / list / logs / start / stop / restart / set-env / delete --yes / next-port`. Decisions worth flagging:
- `delete` is total (route, supervision, logs, AND `projects/<slug>/`). Skill tells the agent to confirm with the user first; `--yes` is required. Trash-bin alternative was rejected — too much complexity for a low-frequency operation.
- `stop` removes the Caddy snippet first (clean 404) then disables the process. Restored on `start`.
- Port allocation is 4000–4019, picked by the CLI (free-port scan in YAML); agent uses `$WEBAPP_PORT` env var in `--command`. 100 ports was the original plan but trimmed to 20 because nono's profile JSON doesn't accept ranges (it's `Vec<u16>`) and 100 entries was JSON noise.
- Readiness probe is an `exec: "bash -c 'echo > /dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/<port>'"` test. process-compose has only `exec` and `http_get` probes — no native `tcp_socket` (a doc-hallucination from an early subagent that got corrected on source inspection).

**Port topology learned the hard way.** Initial deploy crashed: WebUI got `EADDRINUSE` on bind. Cause: containers in this AppTemplate share a network namespace (awsvpc), and **policy-proxy** already listens on `0.0.0.0:8788` in a sibling container — that's the ALB target, and it forwards to `upstream:8787`. So the actual public path is `ALB → policy-proxy:8788 → 8787`. Plan had moved WebUI to 8788; collided. Fix: WebUI moves to **8789**, Caddy owns 8787 (where policy-proxy already forwards). The Caddyfile's catch-all `reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8789` is the WebUI fallback.

**Two more friction points caught in verification.**
1. `webapps` CLI shebang was `#!/usr/bin/env python3` — picked the system python which has no pyyaml. Switched to `#!/opt/hermes/webui/venv/bin/python3` (Hermes's serving venv has pyyaml). Acceptable coupling because the venv is image-owned and stable.
2. Caddy `--watch` was logging `"No files matching import glob pattern"` once per second when `caddy/` was empty (its file scan polls). Seeded a `_placeholder.caddy` no-op snippet on first boot so the glob always matches. (Underscore prefix sorts it first; `*` doesn't match dotfiles, so `.placeholder.caddy` would have been wrong.)

**Phoenix LiveView: `mix phx.server` doesn't work in this sandbox.** Tried as the WS stress test. `mix` calls `Mix.Sync.PubSub` which `:gen_tcp.listen(0, ...)` — random ephemeral port. Nono's listen_port allowlist (`[8787, 8788, 8789, 9956, 4000-4019]`) blocks it: `EACCES`. Source inspection confirmed Mix has no env-var or config to disable Mix.Sync — it's `@moduledoc false` internal. The skill now documents the workaround (`mix release` for production builds, which doesn't trigger Mix.Sync) and adds a generic "EACCES on bind" failure mode note. The architecture itself is fine: Caddy's `reverse_proxy` handles WS upgrades automatically — verified end-to-end with a Python `websockets` echo server (sent "hello"/"world", got "echo: hello"/"echo: world" through Caddy via `ws://127.0.0.1:8787/webapps/ws-echo/`). LiveView would work behind a release build.

**Cold-start verification: persistent-root preserves everything.** Killed the ECS task with `restart-task`; the replacement came up with the previously-created `persist-test` app already `Running` + `Ready` and HTTP 200 served. process-compose.yaml + Caddy snippets + project source all survived in the persistent root.

**Bugfix that landed after merge: cross-origin 403 on POSTs.** First user (`hermes-vmendi00`) hit `POST /api/session/new 403 (Forbidden)` with `Cross-origin request rejected` in the console. Root cause: Caddy's `reverse_proxy` rewrites `Host` to the upstream address by default (Caddy v2 behavior; not v1), so WebUI saw `Host: 127.0.0.1:8789` + `Origin: https://hermes-*.chsandbox.com` and its same-origin CSRF gate rejected the POST. Fix: `header_up Host {host}` in both the Caddyfile fallback and the per-app snippet template. Same gotcha would bite any user web app that gates on origin (Phoenix LiveView's `check_origin`, etc.), so it goes in the snippet template too.

**Key points:**
- Caddy + process-compose, both inside nono. Caddy on 8787 (policy-proxy's upstream); WebUI moves to 8789 to clear 8788 for policy-proxy. process-compose admin API on 9956 (loopback).
- Source-of-truth on the persistent root: `/workspace/webapps/`. Survives container restarts; agent never sees it (uses the `webapps` CLI).
- The CLI is the contract. Mutations are `flock`-protected; readiness is awaited before the Caddy snippet is written; delete is total (with `--yes` + skill-mandated user confirmation).
- Caddy's default Host rewrite breaks same-origin CSRF gates — `header_up Host {host}` is mandatory for any framework that gates on origin (WebUI, Phoenix, etc.). Snippet template includes it by default.
- "Write our own supervisor" was the wrong instinct — process-compose's surgical YAML reload + readiness probes covered everything; ~80 lines of CLI vs 250 lines of bespoke watcher.
- L7 routing decisions are per-request (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive multiplexes paths over one connection; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams). Anything trying to stay out of the data path either pins one backend per connection (breaks the model) or pushes parsing into the kernel (overkill, Fargate-blocked). Caddy in the data path is correct, not a compromise.
- Phoenix dev mode (`mix phx.server`) is incompatible with nono's listen_port allowlist due to `Mix.Sync.PubSub`'s random-port bind. `mix release` works. Documented in the skill as a per-framework gotcha alongside `X-Forwarded-Prefix` config notes.
- `/workspace/webapps/caddy/` needs a placeholder snippet so Caddy's import glob always matches; otherwise `--watch`'s 1Hz file scan spams a warning per second.

## 2026-05-17 23:30 - [Deployment] Drop Hermes sandbox UID to hermeswebui + dedicated user venv

**Conversation:** [2026-05-17-2331-96808b06.md](conversations/2026-05-17-2331-96808b06.md)

Hardened the Hermes runtime sandbox so the LLM can no longer read secrets out of supervisor's outside-the-sandbox daemons, and gave terminal + execute_code a shared, isolated user venv. Triggered by an agent observation about pip cache permissions that turned out to expose a much bigger architectural mistake: the sandbox was running as root.

**The pip-cache thread that started it.** Agent reported `pip install matplotlib` warning that `/workspace/.cache/pip` was not owned by the current user, then later that a package installed via `pip` from `terminal` wasn't importable from `execute_code`. Diagnosis: `tools/code_execution_tool.py:_resolve_child_python` (default `code_execution.mode=project`) walks `$VIRTUAL_ENV` then `sys.executable`. We weren't setting `VIRTUAL_ENV` and the venv's `bin/` wasn't on PATH, so `terminal`'s `pip` resolved to the base image's system Python (`/usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages`) while `execute_code` fell back to `sys.executable` = `/opt/hermes/webui/venv/bin/python`. Two interpreters, two disjoint site-packages.

**The fix shape — dedicated `/workspace/.venv`.** Considered three options: (a) share Hermes's WebUI venv between both tools — rejected because a stray `pip install --upgrade` from the agent could brick Hermes itself; (b) leave the system Python — bad ergonomics, no isolation; (c) carve out a third venv on the persistent volume. Picked (c). Created at image build time via `RUN uv venv --python /usr/local/bin/python3 "${HERMES_WEBUI_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE}/.venv"` in the Dockerfile (right after the WebUI venv install, while still `USER hermeswebui`). At runtime, `supervisor.sh:run_in_nono` exports `VIRTUAL_ENV=/workspace/.venv` and prepends `/workspace/.venv/bin` to PATH, and `hermes-nono-profile.json` adds `VIRTUAL_ENV` to `allow_vars` so it survives nono's env scrub.

**Why Dockerfile and not supervisor.sh ensure-on-boot.** Initially built the venv runtime-side via an `ensure_user_venv` function in supervisor with an existence check, on the (correct) reasoning that the persistent root reuses state across redeploys (`persistent-root-runner.sh:reuse_persistent_root`). User pushed back: "we don't have anything running right now." That makes the upgrade-time argument moot — fresh deploys get the venv via the persistent-root rsync at `initialize_persistent_root`, and existing instances would just need a one-time host wipe of `/var/lib/devopshero/hermes-roots/{slug}` if we ever bump the venv shape. Build-time wins on convention. Confirmed mental model: `/workspace` is rsynced from the image on first boot but reused thereafter — so `/workspace/.venv` from the Dockerfile lands on the persistent volume the same way `/etc` and `/home` do, then survives.

**The bigger discovery — sandbox was running as root.** While planning the venv chown, asked "where do we transition to the hermeswebui user inside the nono sandbox?" Answer: nowhere. `persistent-root-runner.sh:285` exec's supervisor with `HOME=/root USER=root LOGNAME=root`, supervisor stays root, and `nono run` had no `--user` flag and the profile no `"user"` field — so nono inherited root. Probed `hermes-vmendi00` to confirm: from inside Hermes' PID namespace (via `nsenter -t <hermes_pid>`), `cat /proc/<aws_signer>/environ` returned `DOH_ENV_BEARER=...`, `TAVILY_API_KEY=...`, plus the ECS task role's `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI`. `ptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, signer)` returned 0. The sandbox was wide open to its own host.

**Why nono's existing controls didn't save us.** Nono enforced `NoNewPrivs=1`, `Seccomp=2`, and a bounding set dropping `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`/`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. But all 8 namespaces (pid, user, mnt, net, ipc, uts, cgroup, time) were shared with the parent container, AND both supervisor's daemons and the sandbox were UID 0 — so Linux's "you can only ptrace your own UID without `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`" rule never engaged because they had the same UID. The architecture had assumed UID separation; we'd never set it up. Passwordless sudo (`persistent-root-runner.sh:install_passwordless_sudo`) was a red herring — the sandbox didn't need to escalate to read root's environ; it was already root.

**The fix — `runuser -u hermeswebui` wrapping nono.** In `run_in_nono`, the actual nono invocation is now `runuser -u hermeswebui -- "$DOH_BIN_DIR/nono" "${nono_args[@]}" -- /usr/bin/env ...`. Supervisor itself stays root because it's the parent of aws_signer/integrations_broker and needs to signal them at cleanup time (`cleanup` trap). Restructured `main()` into two clearly-labeled stages — Stage 1 root setup (configs, daemons), Stage 2 sandbox prep + drop-and-launch. Added `chown_sandbox_paths` (one-sweep `chown -R hermeswebui:hermeswebui "$HERMES_WEBUI_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE"`) right before `run_in_nono` since everything written above ran as root. Kept passwordless sudo because the user wanted `apt-get install` to keep working — and now sudo-to-root from inside the sandbox doesn't help an attacker because the bounding set already dropped `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` and the same-UID protection still applies for the post-sudo "root" (nono's user namespace maps it to a confined identity, not host UID 0).

**Bonus finding from probing the fixed deploy.** With `runuser` dropping the UID, all 8 namespaces between Hermes and supervisor's daemons now show as DIFFERENT (verified by reading `/proc/<pid>/ns/<ns>`). Nono engages user-namespacing only when invoked as non-root — so we got PID/user/mnt namespace isolation for free as a defense-in-depth layer on top of the UID separation. Three independent controls now block the leak: UID separation, dropped `CAP_SYS_PTRACE`, and namespace isolation.

**One sweep over `/workspace` literals.** While there, replaced hardcoded `/workspace` with `${HERMES_WEBUI_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE}` throughout the Dockerfile (`mkdir`, `chown`, `WORKDIR`, the new venv `RUN`) and `supervisor.sh` (`VIRTUAL_ENV`, PATH). The remaining literal in `hermes-nono-profile.json:43` stays — JSON has no env-var interpolation. Considered making `USER_VENV_DIR` an `ENV` directive in the Dockerfile so both files reference the same source — rejected because globally exporting `VIRTUAL_ENV=/workspace/.venv` would confuse the *outside-sandbox* daemons (they use `$HERMES_WEBUI_PYTHON`, a different venv). Localized to the function body via inline `${HERMES_WEBUI_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE}/.venv`.

**Verification (`hermes-vmendi00`, fresh deploy after teardown).** Process tree shows aws_signer/integrations_broker/supervisor at UID 0; nono and `server.py` at UID 1024. From outside, `runuser -u hermeswebui -- cat /proc/<signer>/environ` → `Permission denied` (was leaking before). From inside sandbox: `VIRTUAL_ENV=/workspace/.venv`, PATH starts with venv `bin/`, `python` resolves to `/usr/local/bin/python3` via the venv's symlink, ownership is `hermeswebui:hermeswebui`. `sudo apt-get install -y tree` succeeded cleanly.

**Key points:**
- Sandbox UID drop is the load-bearing fix; nono's seccomp+caps were necessary but not sufficient because both sides were UID 0.
- `code_execution`'s "project mode" walks `$VIRTUAL_ENV` first — same-process-isolation as terminal but pluggable to a different venv. The two tools share an env when (and only when) we wire it up explicitly.
- Persistent-root + EBS host-mount means runtime ensure-on-boot OR Dockerfile build-time work for `/workspace`; pick build-time when no warm volumes exist, otherwise need both.
- Supervisor must stay root — it owns the credential daemons. Drop happens at the nono boundary specifically, not earlier.
- Passwordless sudo inside the sandbox is fine *now* because `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` is permanently dropped from the bounding set; sudo can grant root locally but can't gain that capability back. Pre-fix, sudo was redundant (already root); post-fix, it's a constrained root.
- The pip cache permissions warning the agent reported was a real symptom of a misconfigured environment; the deeper "two interpreters" diagnosis was correct, and chasing it surfaced the much bigger UID-separation hole.

## 2026-05-17 18:13 - [Deployment] Tighten `hermes_agent` Dockerfile and retire the docker-variant AppTemplates

**Conversation:** [2026-05-17-1815-37d7563d.md](conversations/2026-05-17-1815-37d7563d.md)

Two passes on the Hermes runtime: a small Dockerfile cleanup on the surviving `hermes_agent/` template (with live verification), and the full retirement of the obsolete `hermes-docker-personal` / `hermes-docker-slack` AppTemplates and their `template_repos/hermes_docker_agent/` + `template_repos/doh_dind/` source trees.

**Part 1 — Dockerfile tightening on `template_repos/hermes_agent/Dockerfile`.**

Three targeted edits, all small, plus one regression I introduced and caught in the verification loop:

1. **Line 28** — replaced `ENV PATH=/opt/doh/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/bin:/usr/sbin:/bin:/sbin` with `ENV PATH=${DOH_BIN_DIR}:${PATH}`. The original was duplicating the base image's PATH inline (slightly reordered, with `/usr/local/bin` deduped). Empirically verified the base image (`ghcr.io/nesquena/hermes-webui:0.51.63`) ships `PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin` (including the accidental `/usr/local/bin` duplicate). The new form prepends `$DOH_BIN_DIR` and inherits the rest, so we don't drift from upstream if they change their base PATH.

2. **Lines 56-57** — `RUN echo "export PATH=\"${DOH_BIN_DIR}:\$PATH\"" > /etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh`. Same `DOH_BIN_DIR` consistency nit, but interestingly placed: we want the outer `${DOH_BIN_DIR}` substituted by the Dockerfile's shell at *build* time, but the inner `\$PATH` must stay literal so it's evaluated by the login shell at *boot* time. Switching from single-quoted `'...'` to double-quoted `"..."` plus escaping `\$` gets both. The resulting on-disk file is byte-identical to before. Also explored whether the redundant `chmod 644` on the next line was actually needed — built a throwaway `debian:bookworm-slim` image to confirm BuildKit's default umask is `0022`, which means `echo > file` already produces `644`. The user removed the `chmod 644` line.

3. **Line 110** — dropped `"$DOH_ROOT"` from the build-time `chown -R hermeswebui:hermeswebui ...`. This kept the chown for `$HERMES_ROOT`, `/uv_cache`, `$HERMES_HOME`, and `/workspace` (all genuinely needed by the unprivileged user), but removed it for `/opt/doh`. Rationale: nono's profile (`doh_runtime/hermes-nono-profile.json:46`) already restricts `/opt/doh` to read-only inside the sandbox, so the unprivileged agent never had effective write access anyway. Granting filesystem ownership added zero functionality and made the nono profile the single point of enforcement for "image-owned, not user-modifiable." Now root-ownership backs it up at the filesystem layer too — defense in depth against a future profile typo that swaps `read` for `allow`.

4. **The bug I introduced** — when the user manually removed the `chmod 644` line per (2), they kept the trailing `\` line continuation on the preceding `RUN`. Docker silently merged the `RUN echo ... \` with the next non-blank line, which was a `COPY --chmod=755 build/prune-skills.sh /tmp/prune-skills.sh`. The COPY never executed; the next stage that invoked `/tmp/prune-skills.sh` failed with `not found`. Found this only during the live deploy (build failed), fixed by removing the dangling `\`, redeployed cleanly. Worth remembering: a trailing `\` left behind during a delete is a silent line-merge waiting to happen, and Docker's parser doesn't flag it.

**Live verification flow** (per `template_repos/hermes_agent/AGENTS.md`): started a labelled job worker (`--label dockerfile-cleanup`), deployed `--template hermes-personal` (not `hermes-docker-personal` — see false-start below) into `CH Sandbox / default`, probed the running task with `doh_app_exec`. Confirmed: container default `PATH=/opt/doh/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin` (line 28 effective); `/etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh` contents are literally `export PATH="/opt/doh/bin:$PATH"` with `644` (lines 56-57 effective, umask conjecture confirmed); inside the chroot, `bash -lc 'echo $PATH'` prepends `/opt/doh/bin` after Debian's `/etc/profile` reset (profile.d drop-in survives the reset, which was the whole reason it exists); `/opt/doh` and its scripts owned by `root:root` mode `755`; `sudo -u hermeswebui` successfully runs `nono --version`, `aws --version`, `gws --version` — proving the chown removal doesn't deny the unprivileged user read+execute. WebUI `/health` returned 200. App torn down with `--remove-app --delete-secrets --delete-persistent-data --delete-policies`.

**False start worth recording**: first verification deploy used `--template hermes-docker-personal`. Probe output showed PATH unchanged from the base image and `/opt/doh` not present — which clued me in that the deployed image wasn't built from my modified Dockerfile. Realized `hermes-docker-personal` uses `source_repo_path: "hermes_docker_agent"` (now `deprecated/hermes_docker_agent`), while `hermes-personal` uses `source_repo_path: "hermes_agent"`. Different Dockerfiles. Switched template, redeployed, verification succeeded. Lesson: when verifying a Dockerfile change, sanity-check the deploy targets *that* Dockerfile by inspecting `seed_app_templates.py` first, not just by template-name family resemblance.

**Part 2 — Retired `hermes-docker-personal` and `hermes-docker-slack`.**

The user wanted the docker-variant templates gone but the code retained as reference. Crucially, audited each helper for shared use first — `_HERMES_LLM_VARS`, `_HERMES_TAVILY_VAR`, `_HERMES_AWS_DEFAULT_REGION_VAR`, `_HERMES_CHECKPOINT_EFS_CONFIG`, and `_HERMES_POLICY_PROXY_CONTAINER` are still referenced by the surviving `HERMES_PERSONAL_TEMPLATE` and were kept. Net `seed_app_templates.py` change: -190 lines, surviving template untouched.

Migration state needed a `migrate ... 0056` + `migrate` cycle after the stash dance because reversing-while-stashed leaves the DB row in an applied state without re-running the SQL.

**Key points:**
- Avoid hardcoding paths that are already exposed as `ENV` vars — `${DOH_BIN_DIR}:${PATH}` reads better than the inline `/opt/doh/bin:...:/bin` and inherits future base-image PATH changes for free.
- Double-quoted Dockerfile `RUN echo` strings let you mix build-time substitution (`${DOH_BIN_DIR}`) with login-time literals (`\$PATH`) in one expression — much cleaner than fighting single quotes.
- Defense-in-depth means redundant enforcement: nono restricting `/opt/doh` to read-only is the primary defense, but filesystem ownership by `root` is the second one that catches profile misconfigurations.
- BuildKit's default umask is `0022`. `echo > file` already produces `644`, making `chmod 644` after-the-fact redundant in the common case. Worth knowing before adding extra chmod lines defensively.
- A dangling `\` left after deleting the line below it is a silent Docker line-merge bomb. Docker won't warn; the next non-blank line just gets concatenated. Always check the `\` when you delete the line a continuation feeds into.
- When verifying a Dockerfile change end-to-end, sanity-check which template's `source_repo_path` actually points at the file you modified — template family resemblance is misleading. `hermes-personal` and `hermes-docker-personal` sound paired but build from completely different directories.
- `seed_app_templates` doesn't delete: removing an entry from the seed file just leaves the DB row orphaned. A data migration is the only honest cleanup path if you actually want the row gone everywhere.
- When deprecating a multi-symbol module, audit every helper for shared use before deleting. The `_HERMES_*_VARS` series looked uniform but split cleanly between docker-only (`CREDENTIAL`, `BEDROCK`, `SLACK`, `WEBUI_PASSWORD`, `EFS_CONFIG`) and shared (`LLM`, `TAVILY`, `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`, `CHECKPOINT_EFS_CONFIG`, `POLICY_PROXY_CONTAINER`). Grep is the audit.
- The `template_repos/deprecated/` convention: kept-for-reference dirs live here, no live `source_repo_path` should point at them, a `README.md` indexes what's parked and why. A verbatim `seed_app_templates_excerpt.py` snapshot captures the removed config shape better than a git-blame archaeology trip would.

  - `query=...` — BM25 search across all connectors (default 25, max 100, both bumped from 10/25 by the user after the patch landed).
  - `connector=..., query=""` — enumerate every tool of one connector, alphabetized by `tool_id`, capped at `ENUMERATE_HARD_CAP=500`. This is the new mode for "what can I do with Datadog".
  - `query=..., connector=...` — search filtered to one connector.

  When a known connector is enumerated but disconnected, it falls through to a single `kind="connector"` shell row with the existing "tell the user to open Integrations and click Connect" hint, so the LLM still has a useful answer instead of `[]`.

All 10 probe cases matched expectations including the headline `connector="datadog"` → 50 tools. Test app then torn down via `doh_control teardown-app --remove-app`.

**3. `query_timeseries` and `validate_credential` were flagged `mutates=true`.** The user noticed an LLM aside about it. Root cause: `mutates_from_dash_name` in `connectors/_common.py` walks tokens and matches against `READ_VERBS` / `WRITE_VERBS`; on no-match it defaults to True (the comment makes the rationale explicit — confirmation prompt cheaper than silent mutation). `query` and `validate` weren't in either table, so they fell through. Deleted the copies and imported from `connectors._common`, so the two backends can't drift again. The 24-test `test_mcp_aggregator_state_change` suite still passes.

**4. SOUL and tool-description rewrite.** The original `integrations_search_tools` description told the LLM "search by intent or name," which doesn't teach when to use the new enumerate mode. Rewrote it as a two-mode contract (SEARCH vs ENUMERATE) with default/cap numbers inlined from the constants, and a one-line clarification of `status_filter`. **Key points:**
- `connectedFirst` now does a name tiebreaker. Pure status-sort with no tiebreaker is a code smell — when one branch dominates (all-disconnected), the other branch never runs and the comparator silently does nothing useful.

## 2026-05-16 23:29 - [Integrations] Per-backend, per-transition catalog updates with `authenticated_only` and a `list_tool_catalog` rename

**Conversation:** [2026-05-16-2330-9335825d.md](conversations/2026-05-16-2330-9335825d.md)

Continuation of the earlier session that fixed a stale Merge connector view by adding an `on_config_change` hook on connect and disconnect. The first fix (committed as `c8e5f60`) reloaded the *entire* catalog on every state change, awaited inside the disconnect HTTP handler. That second issue surfaced immediately: clicking Disconnect on Notion appeared to do nothing — the JS `await fetch(.../disconnect)` blocked while the handler awaited a full catalog walk that, among other things, did a `tools/list` against Merge via DOH. By the time the user reloaded the page out of frustration, the panel correctly showed Notion disconnected (the panel reads `oauth.has_token` directly, not the catalog).

The right shape was already implied by the design: refresh only what changed. Two follow-ups landed in this session.

The first follow-up reshaped `on_config_change` from a no-arg notification into a proper state-change message — `(backend_name, connector, transition)` where `transition ∈ {"connected", "disconnected", "reconfigured"}`. A single dispatcher (`MCPAggregator._on_state_change`) decides per transition: disconnects mutate the in-memory store directly via a new `CatalogStore.drop(backend, connector)` (zero network, sub-millisecond, blocks safely); connects and reconfigures schedule a `CatalogStore.reload_backend(backend)` in the background via `asyncio.create_task` so the HTTP response returns immediately. Verified Merge's API has no narrower-than-pack `tools/list` filter — checked the docs at `https://docs.merge.dev/merge-agent-handler/agent-handler/mcp/endpoint-post.mdx` directly. The only relevant filter is the new `?authenticated_only=true` query parameter, which only hides per-connector `authenticate_*` meta-tools and tools whose connectors haven't been authenticated; it doesn't let us scope to one connector. The DCR connectors (Notion, PostHog, Datadog) are single-connector backends where reload-the-whole-backend already equals reload-just-that-connector. Locked the contract with a 24-test unit suite (`test_mcp_aggregator_state_change.py`) covering tool-id collision safety in `drop`, slice-replacement semantics in `reload_backend`, BM25 invalidation, the dispatcher's block-vs-background policy, and the Merge handler firing the right transition values from each upstream response shape.

The second follow-up turned on `?authenticated_only=true` on the upstream MCP relay URL in `merge_handler.integrations_merge_mcp`. Combined with the per-backend reload on `connected`, the agent's tool prompt now contains only what's actually callable — pre-auth, Merge omits the connector's tools server-side; on connect, the dispatcher fires a `reload_backend(merge)` and the next `tools/list` includes them. Removed the in-broker `authenticate_*` filter at the same time: it was a duplicate of what Merge now does server-side, and keeping it as defense-in-depth was rejected per the standing "don't keep unused branches" preference.

Capped the session with a small naming cleanup: `Backend.list_catalog` → `list_tool_catalog`, mirroring the existing `list_known_connectors`. The asymmetry was a real source of confusion — "catalog" reads as the union of tools and connectors at the store level (`CatalogStore` holds both), but at the backend level the same method name only returns tools. Picked the minimal version of the rename: only the methods that are tools-only (`Backend.list_tool_catalog`, `CatalogStore._safe_list_tool_catalog`, `_meta_tool_catalog_entries` in PostHog/Datadog, the test counter). Left store-level names (`CatalogStore`, `CatalogEntry`, `_reload_catalog`, `refresh_catalog`, `/refresh_catalog` URL) alone because they really do operate on the union. The maximally consistent rename — drop "catalog" entirely, call it "integrations" everywhere — was rejected as high-churn for low marginal clarity (the agent-facing tool names already use "integrations", which works).

Verification was static-only by user choice: `py_compile` + the new 24-test suite. Did not run end-to-end against a fresh Hermes container; user opted to verify the Merge connect/disconnect path manually after this commit lands. Open question deferred for that test: how Merge handles public-API connectors (Weather, Wikipedia) under `authenticated_only=true` — the docs don't say whether they count as "always authenticated" (returned) or get hidden until authentication exists for them (filtered out). Worth checking via `integrations_list_connectors` after deploy.

**Key points:**

- The `on_config_change` hook now carries `(backend_name, connector, transition)`. Disconnects mutate the catalog in-place via `CatalogStore.drop` and block; connects/reconfigures schedule a per-backend `reload_backend` in the background.
- `CatalogStore.drop` uses `(backend, connector)` as its filter key, not `tool_id`. Tested explicitly: a same-`tool_id` row in another backend survives the drop.
- `CatalogStore.reload_backend` swaps only the changed backend's slice. Other backends' `list_tool_catalog` is not called — verified via a counter on the test fake. Disappeared connectors get removed; new connectors get added.
- BM25 is invalidated on every state change (drop, reload_backend, full reload) and rebuilt lazily on next `search()`. The store's "tool_count > 0 implies connected" status fixup runs after slice replacement so Merge's public-API connectors stay visible.
- DOH appends `?authenticated_only=true` to the upstream MCP URL. The broker no longer filters `authenticate_*` tools locally; the responsibility is server-side.
- Naming: `list_catalog` was renamed to `list_tool_catalog` only at the backend layer. Store-level names (`CatalogStore`, `_reload_catalog`, `refresh_catalog` and its URL) deliberately left alone because they operate on the tools+connectors union.
- The 24-test suite uses fake backends with mutable state and stubs `fastmcp` / `rank_bm25` when the local venv lacks them, mirroring the pattern in `test_integrations_broker.py`. Tests run via the Django test runner (`uv run manage.py test`).
- Disconnect blocks (sub-millisecond), connect backgrounds (slow upstream). Considered making both async for symmetry; rejected because the asymmetry tracks a real difference (one has network, one doesn't) and uniform-async would introduce a race window where the JS gets `{"ok": true}` but the next agent turn still sees the tool.

## 2026-05-16 20:27 - [Bugfix] Refresh aggregator catalog when a Merge connector is connected mid-session

**Conversation:** [2026-05-16-2028-9335825d.md](conversations/2026-05-16-2028-9335825d.md)

User connected Datadog via Merge.dev's Magic Link in the `hermes-vmendi00` integrations panel. The browser panel correctly showed Datadog as Connected, but the agent reported "Datadog shows `not_connected` with 0 tools available" and asked the user to disconnect/reconnect. Two different data sources, polled on different schedules — and the agent's source had no invalidation hook for the Merge flow.

The browser UI hits `/__doh_broker/integrations` → `aggregator.status_items()`, which currently fetches Merge's connector list live on every panel open and reads `authenticated_connectors` directly off the Registered User record. The agent reads through `CatalogStore`, an in-process cache populated from `backend.list_catalog()` + `backend.list_known_connectors()` and refreshed only on these triggers: boot, the user-facing Refresh button (30s cooldown), DCR OAuth callback success, DCR disconnect, and per-connector `_on_config_change` hooks (PostHog/Datadog meta-tools). Nothing fired the cache invalidation when a Merge connect or disconnect succeeded — so the agent kept seeing the boot snapshot, where Merge's `tools/list` only returned `authenticate_<slug>` tools (filtered out at `mcp_merge_backend.py:142-143`) and `KnownConnector.status` was `not_connected`.

The simplest correct fix reuses the existing `_on_config_change` plumbing the DCR connectors already have: in `MergeBackend`, fire the hook from `handle_connector_status` whenever upstream returns `status=connected` (the JS connect-modal polls every 3s and stops on the first `connected`, so the hook fires exactly once per successful connect) and from `handle_disconnect` on a 200. The aggregator wires the hook to its existing `_reload_catalog`. No JS change, no new endpoint, no cooldown bypass needed (the cooldown only guards the user-facing Refresh button).

Then promoted the hook from a private convention to a first-class part of the `Backend` protocol. The original `MCPAggregator.__init__` had a `hasattr(backend, "_on_config_change")` rewire loop applied only to DCR connectors — Merge would have needed a separate explicit assignment, and Notion would have needed a synthetic no-op default to participate. Cleaner: declare `on_config_change: Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]` on the `Backend` Protocol, make every backend take it as a constructor kwarg (`MergeBackend.__init__`, `DCRConnectorSpec.make_backend(..., on_config_change)`), pass `self._reload_catalog` at construction time, and delete the rewire loop entirely. One pattern, no defaults, no post-hoc attribute mutation, and the hook is documented at the type level.

Verification budget was static checks only (per user choice). Did not run end-to-end against a fresh Hermes container — `template_repos/hermes_agent/AGENTS.md` mandates a from-scratch deploy + browser-driven Magic Link to actually exercise the fix, since redeploying `hermes-vmendi00` boots with Datadog already connected and would not exercise the mid-session reload path. User opted to verify manually after this commit lands.

**Key points:**

- Root cause: `CatalogStore` had no invalidation hook for the Magic Link flow, so a successful Merge connect updated only the live UI path and left the agent's catalog frozen on the boot snapshot.
- Fix exploits the existing JS poll: `MergeBackend.handle_connector_status` fires `on_config_change` on the first `status=connected` response, which is exactly once per successful connect because the modal stops polling at that point.
- `handle_disconnect` mirrors the same hook on a 200 response, so disconnects also reach the catalog without a Refresh click.
- Cleaned up the convention while we were there: `on_config_change` is now a public `Backend` Protocol attribute, every backend takes it as a constructor kwarg, the aggregator passes `self._reload_catalog` at construction, and the `hasattr` rewire loop plus the per-connector `_noop` defaults are gone.
- Static verification: `py_compile` clean across the seven touched files, `git grep` confirmed no `_on_config_change` references survived the rename, no JS or DOH-side changes.
- Did NOT verify end-to-end live; user is verifying manually with a fresh Magic Link connect against a redeployed app.

## 2026-05-16 18:31 - [Bugfix] Restore /opt/doh/bin on PATH for Hermes' login-shell snapshot

**Conversation:** [2026-05-16-1832-174027b0.md](conversations/2026-05-16-1832-174027b0.md)

Started from a user-reported wrong answer in `hermes-datadog-test`: when asked to read emails, the agent replied with a polite "Gmail integration isn't connected — open the Integrations panel and click Connect." Two things smelled off: the Google integration was demonstrably connected (broker `/integrations` reported `status: connected`, refreshed minutes earlier), and the wording the agent used did not appear anywhere in the codebase. The skill (`skills/google-workspace/SKILL.md`) explicitly instructs the agent to surface the broker's verbatim 503 string ("`google integration not connected in DOH — connect it from the Integrations pane.`"), and the broker can only emit that exact phrase. The agent's "Hermes UI", "Integrations **panel**", numbered "click Connect / authorize read permissions" was paraphrase, not a real broker message.

The user then revealed what the agent had actually run: `python /opt/hermes/agent/skills/.../google_api.py gmail search …` returned `FATAL: gws CLI not found in PATH`. So the FATAL was real (one bug), and the agent fabricated the "Gmail isn't connected" rewrite from a vaguely matching error string (a separate, more concerning bug — agent confabulation when stderr says X and the model says "Y is more likely").

**Root cause of the FATAL.** `gws` is installed at `/opt/doh/bin/gws` by our Dockerfile, and `supervisor.sh` exports `PATH=/opt/doh/bin:/usr/local/bin:…` into the nono-sandboxed Hermes process. But Hermes' `LocalEnvironment` builds its terminal session-snapshot with `bash -l -c …` (login shell, see `tools/environments/local.py:389`). Login-shell startup sources Debian's `/etc/profile`, which contains:
```sh
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  PATH="/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
else
  PATH="/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games"
fi
export PATH
```
For `hermeswebui` (uid 1024) this **overwrites** the inherited PATH from scratch. After the snapshot, `/opt/doh/bin` is gone — `shutil.which("gws")` returns `None` → FATAL. `python3` survives because it lives in `/usr/local/bin`. Reproduced directly: `bash -lc 'echo $PATH'` inside nono yields `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games`.

**Fix.** Drop one line into `/etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh` from the Dockerfile, after the existing apt/nono/aws/gws install layer:
```
RUN echo 'export PATH="/opt/doh/bin:$PATH"' > /etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh \
    && chmod 644 /etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh
```
`/etc/profile`'s `run-parts /etc/profile.d/*.sh` loop is Debian-base-files convention and rock-stable. The drop-in adds `/opt/doh/bin` to PATH for any login shell in the image — survives `bash -l`, doesn't touch any file upstream owns, and patches `gws`, `aws`, and any future `/opt/doh/bin/*` tool in one shot.

**Why this respects our update design.** Our customizations of the upstream Hermes image fall into three buckets: (1) patches against upstream code in `build/patches-webui/` and `build/patches-agent/`, applied at image-build via `apply-patches.py`, where a fuzz/reject is a build failure and `hermes-update-check` decides when to retire; (2) DOH-owned files like `doh_runtime/`, `webui-extension/`, `skills/google-workspace/`, copied in via `COPY`; (3) image-layer additions on top of the base — `nono`, `aws`, `gws` installs in the big `RUN` block. `/etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh` is bucket #3: lives in *our* Dockerfile, gets re-laid-down on every rebuild, no upstream-code drift to track. The underlying behavior (login-shell PATH reset) is Debian's design, not Hermes' bug — even if upstream Hermes changed its snapshot mechanism, this drop-in remains the right shape for ensuring `/opt/doh/bin` is on PATH for any login shell.

**End-to-end verification.** Ran the full deploy → boot → agent-runtime loop per `template_repos/hermes_agent/AGENTS.md`: started a labelled worker (`vmendi-doh-bin`), `doh_control deploy-app-template` with the same label spun up `doh-bin-fix-test` in CH Sandbox / default in ~8 min. Then verified inside the live container:
1. `/etc/profile.d/doh-bin.sh` is present and readable.
2. Inside nono as `hermeswebui`, `bash -lc 'echo $PATH; which gws; which aws'` now yields `PATH=/opt/doh/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games` with both binaries resolving — the `/opt/doh/bin` prefix is the addition.
3. `python3 google_api.py gmail labels`, run inside the chroot + nono with the same env vars supervisor.sh injects (`HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:9950`, `SSL_CERT_FILE=/run/doh/integrations-broker/ca/bundle.pem`), returned the owner's actual Gmail labels — system labels (INBOX, SENT, DRAFT, …) and ~16 user-defined labels — through the broker's TLS-intercept token swap. Broker logs show `refreshed google: connected` + `minted leaf cert for www.googleapis.com` with no TLS errors on the success path.

Tore down the test app (`teardown-app --remove-app --delete-persistent-data --delete-policies`) and stopped the labelled worker.

**Key points:**

- The agent confabulation deserves a separate filing. The skill's `SKILL.md:103` already says "surface the broker's 503 verbatim", but the agent rewrote a stderr that didn't even mention auth state into a "Gmail isn't connected" UI prompt. Worth tightening the skill instruction to "do not paraphrase tool stderr; do not infer auth state from anything other than an explicit broker 503."
- `doh_app_exec` lands you in the ALB-target container's mount namespace, *outside* the chroot Hermes runs in (`persistent-root-runner.sh:282` `chroot /hermes-persistent-root …`). The CA bundle that supervisor.sh writes to `/run/doh/integrations-broker/ca/bundle.pem` lives inside the chroot — from `doh_app_exec`'s view it's at `/hermes-persistent-root/run/doh/integrations-broker/ca/bundle.pem`. Reproductions of the agent's exact path need to `chroot /hermes-persistent-root` first, then re-spawn nono. Worth knowing for future debugging.
- Considered a defense-in-depth secondary fix: `HERMES_GWS_BIN=/opt/doh/bin/gws` in the Dockerfile + `allow_vars` in the nono profile (the skill's `google_api.py:46-55` checks this env var before `shutil.which`). Skipped — narrower than the PATH fix (only patches Gmail, not `aws` or any future tool), and only useful as a fallback if PATH gets undone again.
- Considered telling Hermes not to use a login shell for the snapshot (set `terminal.shell_init_files: []`). Rejected — also disables the nvm/pyenv/asdf PATH discovery the login shell deliberately enables.
- `/etc/profile.d/` ordering: if upstream ever ships its own `*.sh` that re-sets PATH, `run-parts` runs alphabetically — could rename ours to `99-doh-bin.sh` to win the ordering. Not needed today.
- Drift-trail: nothing requires `hermes-update-check` to flag this. The fix is image-layer config, not a patch against upstream code.

## 2026-05-16 16:08 - [Integrations] Replaced Hermes broker's timer-driven Google token refresh with lazy-on-demand

**Conversation:** [2026-05-16-1609-9bc45a23.md](conversations/2026-05-16-1609-9bc45a23.md)

User asked whether the broker's ~60-min Google refresh loop could be replaced with a "refresh on 401" approach. We talked through it and rejected 401-driven retry: the broker is a transparent TLS-intercept + header-swap proxy; making it reactive would require buffering request bodies, classifying upstream responses (real auth failures vs. expired-token), and replaying — much more code and many more failure modes than what the timer was buying. Settled on a different simplification: lazy refresh inside `_current_token_for_host`, gated by the existing per-provider lock, with a `REFRESH_LEAD_SECONDS` window so a request never gets a token that expires mid-flight upstream. User accepted that the first-caller-after-expiry blocks for a refresh round-trip (~few hundred ms); skipped the stale-while-revalidate variant because at that point you've reinvented the timer.

**Architectural choices:**

- **One cache, one helper.** Replaced two parallel module-level dicts (`_provider_state` for status rendering + `_host_token` for the proxy) and three coordinator functions (`_refresh_loop`, `_refresh_provider_locked`, `_refresh_all_providers_once`) with a single `_provider_cache` (status + token + monotonic `expires_at` + last-refreshed iso) and one `_ensure_fresh(slug)` helper. The proxy hot path's `_current_token_for_host` now does the host→slug lookup and triggers a refresh inline. Single-flight is preserved by reusing the existing `_provider_refresh_locks` per-provider lock — concurrent first-callers all wait on one in-flight refresh.

- **Collapsed `/integrations/google/kick` into `GET /integrations`.** The kick POST existed solely to bypass the timer-driven cache for the post-OAuth-return case (user clicks Connect, redirects back, but the timer hasn't ticked yet — without kick, UI would show "Not connected" for up to ~60s after a successful connect). Once `_ensure_fresh` is the path, GET can refresh on every render with no staleness window. Deleted the kick endpoint, the WebUI's `kickGoogle()`, and `refreshAfterFlow()`. The post-OAuth return path now just calls `refreshAndRender()` like every other entry point. Tradeoff: every Integrations-tab open hits DOH once per provider; today that's 1 call. Linear scaling with provider count is fine until/unless it becomes a real cost.

- **Folded 5-kind outcomes into a single status string.** Old: `{kind: ok|not_connected|revoked|transient|fatal}`. New: `{status: connected|not_connected|revoked|transient_error}` matching what the WebUI already renders. The proxy's branch on "is there a token" still works — anything not `connected` returns `None`, proxy returns 503. Notably, **401 from the env bearer is now `transient_error` instead of `fatal` (which used to `raise RuntimeError`).** That was safe to change because there's no longer a long-running timer task to crash; a 401 in lazy refresh just means the next request retries. Removes a whole error-propagation path.

- **`_doh_refresh_config` module dict instead of threading args.** The refresh helpers need `(control_plane_url, bearer, owner_username)` from env; threading those three through `_ensure_fresh → _refresh_provider → _fetch_provider_token` from the proxy hot path was noisy. Set once in `_run()`, read inside `_refresh_provider`. Initial naming as `_runtime` was rejected by the user as too generic — renamed to spell out it's the credentials for DOH's per-provider refresh endpoint.

**Verification:**

- Pre-existing test file `devopshero_app/tests/test_integrations_broker.py` can't be loaded by Django's test runner because `mcp_aggregator` imports `fastmcp` which only ships in the Hermes container, not the Django venv. Same on `main`; not introduced here. Worked around with a `sys.modules['mcp_aggregator']` stub for a self-contained smoke test that exercised: lazy first fetch, cache hit across hosts in the same provider, refresh on near-expiry, unknown host short-circuits without a fetch, `not_connected` caches no token, and 20 concurrent first-callers single-flight to one fetch. All pass.
- Updated test file to match new shape — replaced `TestControlKick` with `TestControlIntegrations` (asserts GET refreshes), added `TestLazyTokenForHost` for the lazy-cache scenarios, updated outcome-classification tests to the new `status` values.

**Cleanup:**

- Deleted dead constants: `MIN_SLEEP_SECONDS`, `NOT_CONNECTED_POLL_SECONDS`, `BACKOFF_INITIAL_SECONDS`, `BACKOFF_MAX_SECONDS`. Backoff jitter is gone — there's no loop to back off in.
- Updated `google_oauth.py` disconnect docstring (referenced the dead `/kick` endpoint).
- Updated `patches-webui/07-doh-broker-proxy.patch` comment that mentioned kick.

**Net diff:** −56 lines in the broker, similar reductions in the WebUI extension. Total ~220 insertions / ~276 deletions across 5 files.

## 2026-05-16 13:10 - [Integrations] DCR candidate audit — per-vendor reports + summary for the next-wave direct integrations

**Conversation:** [2026-05-16-1310-30f95663.md](conversations/2026-05-16-1310-30f95663.md)

This session started as a one-shot question — "list Merge connectors that follow the Notion DCR model" — and walked through three rounds of methodology correction before landing on a proper two-axis audit, then expanded into a full per-vendor research pass for the next-wave integrations after PostHog.

**Three methodology errors caught by the user, in order.** Each one tightened the criterion:

1. **First pass**: I scanned `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` for a `registration_endpoint` and called everything with one a "DCR candidate." This put Vercel in the list. 2. **Second pass**: With the new filter Vercel was out, but the user pulled Datadog's Merge connector card and pointed out it's `API key + application key`, not OAuth. Yet I had Datadog in Group 1 because `mcp.datadoghq.com` advertises DCR. The user's pushback was sharper: I was conflating two questions. "Does the vendor expose an official MCP server with DCR somewhere?" is about the vendor's roadmap. "How does Merge integrate this connector today?" is about Merge's chosen mechanism. They are independent. I admitted the bug, restructured the doc into two parts (Part 1: how Merge integrates each connector. Part 2: which vendors host their own DCR-capable MCP). Renamed `merge_connectors_dcr_audit.md` → `merge_connectors_auth_audit.md`.
3. **Third pass**: Datadog's protocol surface is genuinely Notion-shape — empty `scopes_supported`, valid DCR returning a `client_id`, no allowlist hint in the WWW-Authenticate. So why does Merge pick API key? **Most likely API surface coverage** — Merge's 49 Datadog tools cover the basics; Datadog's first-party MCP exposes 110+ across 18 toolsets including APM, logs, error-tracking, security, llmobs that Merge omits. Merge's choice is about what their REST integration can deliver uniformly, not about DCR being unusable.

**The PostHog comparison cemented the conclusion.** PostHog has DCR + a full first-party MCP with **~350 tools, 171 fine-grained scopes, and three URL-level narrowing knobs** (`?features=`, `?tools=`, `organization_id` / `project_id`). Merge ships **63 tools** for PostHog using API key paste. Merge isn't bad — they cover everyday admin CRUD across all 151 connectors with one auth model. They're not best-in-class for any specific vendor; they're best-in-class for breadth + uniformity. That trade-off matters for the next-wave integration plan.

**The next-wave audit (the heart of this session).** User asked: for every Group 1 vendor that follows the PostHog pattern, do the same investigation we did for PostHog. Produce a per-vendor file plus a summary, persisted to `docs/`. 25 vendors (27 minus Notion + PostHog, with Atlassian's three Merge connectors collapsed to one Atlassian file). Workflow: triage with `curl` against each AS metadata + protected-resource doc + a live POST to `/register` to confirm DCR still issues `client_id`s; tabulate Merge tool counts from the cached `/tmp/merge_pages/`; dispatch four parallel `general-purpose` research agents, each owning ~6 vendors, to fetch official MCP docs and answer a structured set of questions (tool count, scope shape, session-narrowing knobs, multi-tenancy, novelty quirks, status, sources); synthesize per-vendor reports following a consistent template; write a SUMMARY.md with tier ranking and an inventory of mechanisms still missing from the aggregator.

**Why a connector spec module per vendor, not a config table.** The PostHog worktree (`.claude/worktrees/posthog-mcp/`) introduced a `DCRConnectorSpec` dataclass and one self-contained module under `connectors/<slug>.py` per DCR vendor — Notion and PostHog already there, the aggregator iterates `DCR_CONNECTORS` at boot to build providers and backends. The audit confirmed this shape is right: every vendor has at least one quirk (workspace baked into token, two-host OAuth, sandbox vs prod, region picker, scope tier, BYO endpoint, dynamic tool list) that doesn't fit a uniform table. Each connector module gets to encode its own scope string, mutation overrides, and any meta-tools for per-session config without polluting siblings.

**Why I didn't try to drive a full PKCE handshake against any vendor.** Tempting to validate end-to-end before declaring each vendor a candidate, but practically intractable for 25 vendors in one pass. The published metadata + a successful `client_id` return is the right *floor* for the audit; anyone moving to implementation is told to "drive Magic Link once and confirm" before declaring victory. Captured this as a caveat in the audit doc and the SUMMARY.

**Tier ranking by ratio of customer value to engineering work, not by alphabetical order or scope complexity.** Tier 1 are pure Notion-shape and validate the connector module pattern across new vendors (linear, asana, contentful, sanity, monday). Tier 2 introduce `default_scope` strings — first time we exercise that field with non-trivial values (miro, stripe, canva, airtable, attio, atlassian). Atlassian gets time pressure: the `/v1/sse` endpoint sunsets 2026-06-30, hard deadline. Tier 3 are full PostHog-shape needing per-session config and meta-tools — datadog (the most direct PostHog clone, ?toolsets=, regions), klaviyo (lighter, two boolean toggles + ?company), make (most novel: scenarios-as-tools = dynamic tool list per session + async execution beyond MCP timeout), paypal (header-based config not query-string), sentry (the most sophisticated of all — layered OAuth, path-based scoping, skills system, embedded agents), gitlab (heaviest — self-managed instance URLs, 26 scopes, dual endpoints).

**Mechanisms inventory for what's still missing in the aggregator.** PostHog's worktree handles `default_scope`, per-session config, meta-tools, and dynamic upstream URL rebuild. The Tier 3 vendors require capabilities the worktree doesn't yet have: region picker at consent (Datadog has six, no central router; Sentry/GitLab self-hosted are arbitrary URLs); per-session HTTP headers, not just URL params (PayPal); disable tool-list caching for dynamic connectors (Make's scenarios, Figma's plan-conditional visibility); async execution beyond MCP timeout (Make's 40-min scenario runs return `executionId` for follow-up polling); configurable upstream host per connection; two-connector pattern for sandbox vs production (Stripe, PayPal); allowlist-precondition signaling (Square, ClickUp, Ramp, Figma). The final two-part doc structure separates "what does Merge do for this connector?" (Part 1) from "does the vendor host its own DCR-capable MCP?" (Part 2), with Part 3 cross-cutting them.

Bundling Atlassian's three connectors into one batch saved cycles. The agents pulled official docs (vendor-controlled URLs only — `developers.figma.com`, `support.atlassian.com`, `docs.stripe.com`, `developers.intercom.com`, etc.), enumerated tool surfaces verbatim where published, and flagged sparse-docs vendors honestly rather than padding. This makes the dir scannable for someone deciding which integration to build next: open a file, get the verdict in under a minute. The SUMMARY tier table rolls them up; mechanisms-still-required section is the hand-off to whoever owns aggregator work.
- Square / ClickUp / Ramp / Figma all have **redirect-URI allowlists** even though their DCR endpoints work. Aggregator can detect this — DCR succeeds, OAuth authorize step rejects unknown URIs — but we should surface "this client must be allowlisted by <vendor>" in the integrations panel rather than letting the user see a generic OAuth failure. New design item for the integrations broker.
- Two unexpected finds: (1) Make.com's **scenarios-as-tools** is the most dynamic mechanism in the audit — your active on-demand scenarios become MCP tools, names + schemas derived from each scenario's configuration. Per-session tool discovery, no caching. Even more dynamic than PostHog's session-config narrowing. (2) Sentry's **path-based session scoping** (`/mcp`, `/mcp/:org`, `/mcp/:org/:project`) is novel — the OAuth `resource` parameter binds the issued token to that path, and tokens cannot be reused against a broader path. Closer to capability-based security than to scope strings.
- Notion + PostHog excluded from this audit by design. Notion is already integrated; PostHog is the worktree-in-flight. The audit is explicitly the *next* wave.
- Caveats noted in the doc: the Tool Pack catalog drifts (this is a 2026-05-16 snapshot); DCR existing at the protocol level is necessary but not sufficient (Vercel proved this); some "scopes_supported = []" vendors really are coarse (Notion, Linear), others have scopes enforced server-side (Klaviyo's role-gating, Datadog's `mcp_read`/`mcp_write` RBAC); enterprise allowlists by client_id (Airtable) need a different path than public DCR.

## 2026-05-15 23:39 - [DevEx] Per-worker label scoping for parallel-worktree verification

**Conversation:** [2026-05-15-2340-74f0749e.md](conversations/2026-05-15-2340-74f0749e.md)

The Hermes verification flow in `template_repos/hermes_agent/AGENTS.md` told Claude to *stop* any running `run_job_worker` and start a fresh one in its worktree before deploying. That works for one Claude at a time but breaks the moment two Claudes work in parallel — they keep killing each other's workers, and a stale main-tree worker can still race ahead and claim a job created from a worktree (the worker imports its code at process-start, so it executes whichever code its own worktree was on when started). Replaced "kill the others" with "scope your own work so others can't see it."

**Why a label, not a per-app `--app` filter.** First idea was `run_job_worker --app foo`. Two problems: (1) other unscoped workers (the host main-tree worker) still grab `foo`'s rows because `skip_locked=True` is per-row, not per-app — so we'd be back to telling Claudes to stop the main worker; (2) it doesn't generalize cleanly to environment-level jobs or multi-app verification flows. A free-form `App.label` field — defaulting to `""` for everything UI-created — lets the unscoped main worker only see `label=""` rows, and a labelled worker only see its own. They literally cannot collide.

**Why `App.label` and not `Deployment.label` or `Blueprint.label`.** A verification session orbits one App: deploy → maybe redeploy → maybe permission-apply → teardown → remove. Stamping on the App means every downstream row (Deployment, AppPermissionRequest, AppRemovalJob) inherits the scope transitively through the FK. We only need to plumb a `--label` flag through *one* command — `doh_control deploy-app-template`, which is the only thing creating new Apps from the CLI — and every other operation reads it for free. That's the difference between "two new flags and one model field" and "label parameter on every job-creating service in the codebase."

**The AppRemovalJob subtlety I got wrong twice.** First claimed the App row could be gone by the time the removal job is claimed (so we'd need a `label_snapshot` field). User pushed back, and re-reading `app_remove_executor.run_removal` made it obvious: `app.delete()` runs at the very *end* of the executor, long after the worker has claimed the job. The App is always present at claim time. The removal job's existing `app_id_snapshot` field (a UUID, not a FK — it has to survive the eventual `app.delete()` for audit) is fine for the claim filter: `.filter(app_id_snapshot__in=App.objects.filter(label=label).values("id"))`. No extra schema change.

**Env-level jobs (provisioning/teardown) stay unscoped.** They have no FK to App, and a verification session usually reuses an existing env. Adding `Environment.label` would force a label decision into env-creation flows that are otherwise invariant across worktrees. Decided: env-level claims are gated by `if not label:` in the worker loop, so a labelled worker simply skips them. The unscoped main worker handles all env work for everyone. If env-creation collisions become a real problem someday, we can revisit; today they aren't.

**Magic-via-env-var idea was rejected for being too magical.** Considered using `os.environ["DOH_WORKER_LABEL"]` plus a `pre_save` signal so callers wouldn't need to plumb the parameter at all — both the worker and `deploy-app-template` would inherit it from the shell. Zero callsite changes, but the coupling is invisible: a future reader sees a `label` column and has to grep the codebase to discover the env-var hook. Explicit beats magic here, especially since the only places that actually need to set it are `deploy_from_template` (CLI passes label, UI passes `""`) and `start_worker` (management command passes label, AppConfig.ready passes `""`).

**Key points:**
- The right unit of scoping is the *resource that's being verified*, not the worker process or the job row. Workers and jobs are ephemeral; the App outlives them and naturally carries verification identity through to every dependent row via FK.
- Unscoped (`label=""`) is a real production state, not a placeholder. The web-server-embedded worker (`apps.py`) and the host main-tree CLI worker both run unscoped and serve real users; the labelled mode is purely a developer-affordance overlay. This is why the field is `default=""` and not nullable — `""` is the meaningful "main worker territory" value, distinct from "we forgot to think about this."
- Resisted plumbing `--label` into `redeploy-app`, `teardown-app`, etc. The label is a property of the App, not of each invocation. Once stamped at app creation, it's the worker's job (literally) to filter by it — callers shouldn't have to think about it again.
- The fix is mostly subtractive: instead of orchestrating "everyone stop their workers before I run mine," we let workers stay running indefinitely and use the schema to make their visibility cones non-overlapping.

User pointed out `partial(self._refresh_access_token, slug=spec.slug)` is one line, idiomatic, and captures by value at construction time without any closure-scoping ceremony. Helper deleted, callsite collapsed.

**Decoupled the broker from Merge entirely.** The unified `/__doh_broker/integrations` fan-out in the broker called `aggregator.merge_backend.handle_connectors(request)` directly, reaching through a public property to invoke a Merge-specific handler. Replaced with a new `aggregator.status_items(request)` that returns a flat `list[dict]` of ready-to-render cards — one entry per DCR provider plus one per Merge-managed connector. The aggregator already knew about both kinds of providers, so it owns the assembly. Broker now does `items.extend(await aggregator.status_items(request=request))` and stops knowing Merge or Notion or PostHog exist as concepts. The `merge_backend` property and the old `handle_status` Response wrapper both went away. JSON encode/decode round-trip between aggregator and broker also gone.

**Moved `sys.path.insert` from the production broker module to the test fixture.** `integrations_broker.py` had `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent))` at module top so `import mcp_aggregator` would resolve. User flagged it as cognitive load: anyone reading the file had to evaluate and dismiss the line. Production path (supervisor.sh runs the broker as a script) already gets `/opt/doh/runtime/` on sys.path automatically. The only execution context that needs the manual insertion is `devopshero_app/tests/test_integrations_broker.py`, which loads the broker via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` from outside the runtime dir. Moved the insertion into that fixture's `_load_broker_module()` helper. Broker module is now clean.

**Moved `mcp_aggregator` import out of the deferred position.** Was inside `_run()` to defer heavy imports until the broker actually started. User asked why; investigation showed there's no concrete reason — the broker is the only entrypoint, deferring just shifts the failure point from line 1 to line 937. Hoisted to the top with the other imports; dropped the three string forward-ref type annotations (`aggregator: "mcp_aggregator.MCPAggregator"`) to plain references. Cleaned up three pre-existing ruff F401/F841 warnings in the broker (unused `socket`, `time`, `has_cl`) while we were touching the file.

**Renamed `merge_backend.py` → `mcp_merge_backend.py`.** Visual symmetry with `mcp_aggregator.py` and `mcp_top_level_tools.py`. The three modules now group together when listing the runtime directory.

**Verified end-to-end** on a fresh deploy of `hermes-posthog` to CH Sandbox using the new `App.label` per-worker scoping protocol that landed in main while this work was happening (commit `b320783`). Stamped `App.label = "posthog-mcp"` on the existing row, ran `run_job_worker --label posthog-mcp` from the worktree alongside any other workers (none collided), redeployed. Container at https://hermes-posthog.chsandbox.com confirms: top-level FastMCP exposes the same 4 `integrations_*` tools, `/__doh_broker/integrations` returns the same shape (1 TLS intercept + 2 MCP aggregator + 151 Merge connectors), PostHog stays connected with its 200+ tools, the three `posthog-*` meta-tools still surface in `integrations_search_tools` queries.

**Key points:**

- **Each cleanup was small. The pattern was the bigger lesson.** A defensive `sys.path.insert` "in case the broker is loaded from elsewhere." A closure factory "to make the late-binding fix explicit for future readers." A legacy dict "kept around so OAuth handlers don't need rewriting." A property exposing `merge_backend` "so the broker can fan out cleanly." Each one read like a reasonable hedge in isolation and added cognitive tax in aggregate. User caught all of them in this session by selecting individual lines and asking "why is this here?" — that's a much higher-bandwidth review pattern than "review the whole file."
- **Removing duplicate state always beats apologizing for it.** The legacy `MCP_PROVIDERS` dict had a comment explaining why it existed. Six small edits later, both the dict and the comment were gone. Same data, one representation, no comment needed.
- **`functools.partial` is the right tool for late-binding loops.** Not a lambda with a default-argument trick (`lambda s=x: ...` works but reads as "weird default value"), not a closure factory (`def _make_fn(slug): ...` works but reads as "why isn't this a lambda"). `partial` is the standard library's answer to exactly this problem and doesn't carry the "wait, why isn't this simpler?" smell.
- **The aggregator should own "what integrations exist and what's their status."** The broker's job is HTTP; it shouldn't know Merge or Notion or PostHog by name. Existing app row didn't have a label, but stamping it via `App.objects.get(slug=...).label = "..."` was the same one-line shell update we'd have needed for any pre-existing row, and the labelled worker took it from there. Compared to the prior session's "kill the main worker, start one in the worktree, race conditions if you forget" — much better.
- **Ruff is now clean across all runtime modules.** Five files in `doh_runtime/` (aggregator, top-level tools, merge backend, broker, connectors package). Previously had 6 errors in the broker that were entirely pre-existing housekeeping; addressed in passing while the file was already open.

Caught this in production: first deploy returned `502 failed to fetch OAuth metadata` until the fix went out.
